stem: Observations x1, x2, ..., xn have geometric mean G. If every observation is multiplied by a constant k > 0, what is the geometric mean of the new data set?

per_option_rationale.rationale: New GM = (k^n * product(xi))^(1/n) = k * (product(xi))^(1/n) = k * G. Multiplying all values by k scales the GM by k.
G^k confuses the effect of a change of scale on GM with an exponentiation; a student who takes log(GM) = k*log(G) (incorrectly treating multiplication by k as raising to the power k) arrives at G^k.

G + k applies the change-of-origin rule to GM (which correctly holds for AM under a shift), but GM under a scale change is a multiplicative, not additive, transformation; a student who confuses AM shift with GM scale gets G + k.
k^n * G results from taking the nth root only partially: new product = k^n * product(xi), and a student who forgets to apply the nth root to the k^n factor reports k^n * G instead of k * G.

explanation: GM of (k*x1, k*x2, ..., k*xn) = (k^n * x1*x2*...*xn)^(1/n) = k^(n/n) * (x1*...*xn)^(1/n) = k * G. Multiplying all observations by a constant k multiplies the GM by k.

explanation_sections.punchline: Multiplying every observation by k raises the entire product to involve k^n, and taking the nth root recovers exactly one factor of k, giving new GM = k * G.
explanation_sections.approach: State the property: GM scales with a change of scale. For GM: new_GM = (k^n * prod)^(1/n) = k * G. Contrast the confusable rule: for AM, adding a constant c to every value shifts AM by c (AM + c). For GM, multiplying by k scales GM by k.
explanation_sections.lesson: GM satisfies: (1) scale change by k -> GM multiplied by k; (2) origin shift by c -> no clean formula (GM is NOT additive). Contrast with AM: origin shift by c adds c to AM.
explanation_sections.timing: About 60 seconds. This is a property/concept item. Eliminate option 3 (AM-type shift rule) and option 4 (forgot the nth root) quickly.
